place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 山门外的林子
place.en: Chending Temple · the woods outside the gate

setup.zh: 三试，胆子：林子里一只蠪侄，九首九尾，虎爪，叫声像婴儿，拴在古松上。一半的孩子哭着跑了。
setup.en: Third trial, nerve: in the woods a Longzhi — nine heads, nine tails, tiger claws, a cry like an infant's — chained to an old pine. Half the children run away crying.

recap.zh: 三试，胆子：你听出了蠪侄九个头里哪一个是真的；它扑来的那一刻，木牌一烫——「……左边」。
recap.en: Third trial, nerve: you heard which of the Longzhi's nine heads was real; as it lunged, the token burned — "…Left."

zh: 九首，九尾，虎爪；其音如婴儿。
锁链够不着的地方，站着一个人。
en: Nine heads, nine tails, tiger claws; a voice like an infant.
Just beyond the chain's reach, someone stands.

story.zh:
**三试 · 胆子。**

二试下来，剩了不到三百人。马小宝的考牌上是一个圈，照理不能再往下考了。马三挤到执事跟前，把那封盖着县衙大印的信又亮了一亮。执事看看信，又朝正殿那边望了一眼，没有说话，放他进了队。

三试考的地方，在山门外西边的一片老林子里。林子里的树，一棵比一棵老，一棵比一棵黑，大白天走进去，也像走进了傍晚。林子正中是一棵古松，松树底下，拿一根比人腿还粗的铁链，拴着一只妖兽，叫作蠪侄。它身子像狐狸，却比牛还大；九个脑袋，九条尾巴，四只爪子是虎的爪子。九个脑袋一齐转过来，盯着每一个走进林子的孩子；九张嘴一齐张开，叫起来像九个婴儿在同时哭，哭声在林子里撞来撞去，撞得人头皮发麻，脚底发软。

执事站在林子口，道：「进去。走到古松底下，摸一下松树皮，出来。一个一个进。」头一个进去的孩子，走了不到十步，便哭着跑了出来。第二个走了五步。第三个站在林子口，腿抖了半天，一步也没迈进去，给他爹从人群里拽走了。

排队的时候，早上指着小满那张弓笑的那个穿绸衫的孩子，家里请过先生，这时候见大家都怕，便要显一显本事，摇头晃脑地背道：「有兽焉，其状如狐，而九尾、九首、虎爪，名曰蠪侄，其音如婴儿——」背到这里，他顿住了。旁边一个孩子问：「其音如婴儿，然后呢？」那穿绸衫的孩子脸色慢慢地白了，嘴唇哆嗦了两下，才把最后三个字挤出来：「……是、食、人。」四下里登时一片死寂。过了一会儿，不知是谁先「哇」的一声哭了出来，跟着便哭成了一片，那穿绸衫的孩子自己哭得最响。这几句出自《山海经》，一字不差，那孩子的先生教得好。只是先生大约没有教过他，有些书，背到最后三个字，要看看场合。

马小宝进去了。他走了三步。第三步落地的时候，蠪侄的九个脑袋一齐转向了他。马小宝站住了，一动不动，好一会儿，林子外头的人都瞧见，他那条绸裤子的裤腿底下，慢慢地洇开了一滩水。两个家丁冲进林子，一左一右把他抬了出来。马小宝给抬在半空里，两条腿乱蹬，嘴里还在喊：「我没有！是露水！是露水！」林子外头的人，这一回谁也憋不住了。只有一个人没有笑，是马三。他一张脸先是红，再是紫，再是黑，最后变成了一种蒙山上的人都认得的颜色——「完了」色。

马三却没有走。他站在人堆里，眼睛从儿子湿了的裤子上挪开，一寸一寸地挪，挪到了排在队尾的小满身上。他招手叫过葛六，低声说了几句。葛六的脸色变了一变，摇了摇头。马三又说了一句，从怀里摸出一锭银子。葛六看了那锭银子很久，没有接。马三的脸沉了下来，道：「那五两，你也别要了。」葛六没说话，转身挤出人群走了。马三便把那锭银子塞给了身边一个家丁。

轮到小满之前，他在林子外头等了将近一个时辰。别的孩子等的时候，有的在哭，有的闭着眼睛念佛，有的抓一把土往自己脸上抹，说是抹了土，妖怪便闻不出人味——这也是那卖登仙符的教的，另收五文。小满什么也没做。他就蹲在林子边上，歪着头，听。只有一回，他抬了抬眼：一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘走进了林子，闭着眼睛，一步一步，不快不慢，走到古松底下摸了一把树皮，又闭着眼睛走了出来，从头到尾没看那兽一眼。九个脑袋冲她哭了一路，她像是没听见。小满心想：这是个狠人。

他爹教过他，怎么分狼嚎和风声：狼嚎是从胸口里出来的，是热的；风只有一个洞，再响也是空的。他听了一个时辰。那九个脑袋叫一回，他听一回。听到后来，他发觉一桩怪事：每回九张嘴一齐张开，九种哭声一齐涌出来，林子深处那棵古松的松针，只跟着其中一种哭声抖。别的八种，哭得再响，松针一动也不动。

轮到他了。他走进林子，没有往前冲，站在铁链够不着的地方，站定了，闭上了眼睛。九种哭声，一齐涌进他耳朵里来。他一种一种地听。第一种，是空的，像风灌进一只破瓦罐。第二种，也是空的，像有人对着一口枯井喊了一声，井底下应回来的那一声。第三种、第四种、第五种、第六种、第七种，空的。第九种，空的。只有第八种，不是。第八种是从胸腔里出来的，一呼一吸之间，带着热气，带着一股说不出的腥，还带着一点——小满后来想了很久，才想出一个词来——饿。那是一种很深很深的饿，饿得发慌，饿得不管不顾，好像把整座林子吃下去，把整座山吃下去，也不会饱。另外八个，都是它的影子。

他睁开眼睛，弯下腰，从地上捡起了一块石头。
story.en:
**Third trial · Nerve.**

After the second trial, fewer than three hundred were left. Ma Xiaobao's tag had a circle on it; by rights he couldn't go on. Ma San pushed up to the steward and showed the letter with the county seal once more. The steward looked at the letter, glanced toward the main hall, said nothing, and let him into the line.

The third trial was held in an old forest west of the gate. Each tree older and darker than the last; walking in at noon was like walking into dusk. In the middle stood an old pine, and under it, on an iron chain thicker than a man's leg, was chained a demon beast called the Longzhi. Its body was like a fox's but bigger than an ox; nine heads, nine tails, and four tiger's claws. The nine heads all turned to stare at every child who walked into the forest; the nine mouths opened together, and its cry was like nine infants wailing at once, knocking about the forest till your scalp crawled and your feet went soft.

A steward stood at the edge of the forest. "In you go. Walk to the old pine, touch the bark once, come out. One at a time." The first child in got less than ten steps and came running out in tears. The second got five. The third stood at the edge, legs shaking a long while, never took a step, and was hauled away by his father from the crowd.

While they queued, the boy in silk who had pointed at Xiaoman's bow that morning — his family had hired a tutor — seeing everyone afraid, decided to show off, and recited with a wag of his head: "There is a beast, shaped like a fox, with nine tails, nine heads and tiger's claws, called the Longzhi; its cry is like an infant's —" There he stopped. A child beside him asked: "Its cry is like an infant's — and then?" The silk-gowned boy's face slowly went white; his lips trembled twice before he squeezed out the last three words: "…it — eats — people." Dead silence all round. After a moment someone went "Waaah!" and then they were all crying, the silk boy loudest of all. The lines were from the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, word for word — his tutor had taught him well. Only the tutor had probably never taught him that with some books, before the last three words, you look at where you are.

Ma Xiaobao went in. He went three steps. As the third foot landed, the Longzhi's nine heads all turned toward him together. Ma Xiaobao stood still, not moving, for a good while, and everyone outside the forest saw a puddle slowly spread beneath the legs of his silk trousers. Two servants rushed in and carried him out between them. Hoisted in mid-air, legs kicking, he was still shouting: "I didn't! It's dew! It's dew!" This time nobody outside could hold it in. Only one man didn't laugh: Ma San. His face went first red, then purple, then black, and at last a colour everyone on Mount Meng knew — "done for".

But Ma San didn't leave. He stood in the crowd, and his eyes moved off his son's wet trousers, inch by inch, until they reached Xiaoman at the end of the line. He beckoned Ge Liu over and said a few words low. Ge Liu's face changed; he shook his head. Ma San said one more thing and took out a silver ingot. Ge Liu looked at the ingot a long time, and didn't take it. Ma San's face darkened. "Those five taels — you can forget them too." Ge Liu said nothing, turned, and pushed his way out of the crowd. Ma San put the ingot into the hand of a servant beside him.

Before his turn, Xiaoman waited outside the forest for the better part of two hours. The other children, waiting, cried, or prayed to the Buddha with their eyes shut, or grabbed handfuls of earth and smeared it on their faces — smear on earth and the monster can't smell a person, they said; that too was the charm seller's teaching, five coppers extra. Xiaoman did nothing. He squatted at the edge of the forest, head cocked, and listened. Only once he looked up: a girl with two little braids walked into the forest with her eyes closed, step by step, neither fast nor slow, walked to the old pine, touched the bark, and walked out again with her eyes closed, never once looking at the beast. The nine heads wailed at her the whole way, and she seemed not to hear. Xiaoman thought: now that one's tough.

His father had taught him how to tell a wolf's howl from the wind: a howl comes out of a chest, it's warm; the wind has only a hole, and however loud, it's hollow. He listened for two hours. Each time the nine heads cried, he listened. In the end he noticed something strange: each time the nine mouths opened together and nine cries poured out, the needles of the old pine deep in the forest trembled with only one of them. The other eight, however loud, never stirred a needle.

His turn came. He walked into the forest, didn't rush forward, stopped where the chain couldn't reach, stood still, and closed his eyes. The nine kinds of crying poured into his ears together. He listened to them one by one. The first was hollow, like wind blowing into a cracked jar. The second was hollow too, like someone shouting into a dry well and the well shouting back. The third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh — hollow. The ninth, hollow. Only the eighth was not. The eighth came out of a chest; between breaths it carried heat, a rankness he couldn't name, and something — Xiaoman thought a long time afterward before he found the word — hunger. A very deep hunger, frantic, reckless, as if it could eat the whole forest, the whole mountain, and not be full. The other eight were all its shadows.

He opened his eyes, bent down, and picked a stone up off the ground.

exits.means: fights the Longzhi, takes the third trial

withdrawn.zh: 蠪侄缩回古松后面，九个头龇着牙。瞿老：「再来。」
withdrawn.en: The Longzhi shrinks back behind the pine, nine heads baring their teeth. Elder Qu: "Again."

story.zh:
就在这时，林子外头「嗖」的一声，一颗石子从人堆里飞进来，不偏不倚，打在蠪侄的后腿上。那兽吃了痛，九个脑袋一齐昂起，铁链「哗啦」一声绷得笔直，古松都给扯得晃了一晃——它没有去扑那扔石子的人。它扑向了离它最近的那一个。

一只虎爪带着风，劈头盖脸地朝小满扫过来。便在这时，他胸口那块木牌忽然一烫，烫得他心口一跳，一个很小、很困、像是从极深极深的地方浮上来的声音，在他耳朵里道：

⟪「……左边。」⟫

他想也没想，往右一滚。那虎爪擦着他的左肩扫了过去，扫断了他身后一棵碗口粗的小松树，「咔嚓」一声，松树倒了，松针落了他一头一脸。他趴在地上，心里想：你爷爷的，九个脑袋。他手里那块石头，却已经出手了——不偏不倚，正正地砸在第八个脑袋的鼻尖上。

蠪侄登时愣住了。它那一扑的势子，在半空里停了一停，像是忽然忘了自己要做什么。然后，另外八个脑袋，一下子散了，像一口哈在冬天窗户上的热气，眨一眨眼，便什么都没有了。林子里只剩下一只狐狸模样的兽，一个脑袋，一条尾巴，比牛还大，却捂着鼻子，委委屈屈地「呜」了一声，夹着尾巴，缩回古松后面去了。林子里忽然很静。

小满从地上爬起来，拍了拍身上的松针，回头一看：林子口拄着扫帚站着那个扫地的老头，也不知站了多久，看了多久。老头脚边，马家那个家丁坐在地上，抱着自己的右手腕，疼得直抽冷气，也不知是怎么扭着的。那把扫帚，没有在扫。

小满摸了摸胸口的木牌。它又凉了，凉得像从来没有热过。他小声道：「……谢了。」木牌没有回答。他又小声道：「……记账？」木牌，轻轻地，暖了一下。

他这才想起来，三试的题目，是摸一下松树皮。他便走过去。古松后头，蹲着那只只剩一个脑袋的兽，拿两只虎爪捂着鼻子，一双湿漉漉的眼睛从爪缝里往外瞅着他，倒有几分像村口老周家那条挨了打的黄狗。小满伸手摸了摸松树皮，蹲下来，隔着一步远，道：「对不住。砸疼了吧。」那兽没作声，把捂着鼻子的爪子，放下来了一点点。它的鼻头给砸得通红，红得像一根萝卜。

这个听声的法子，沈小满这一辈子，后来又用过一回。那一回，也是九个头，也是八个空的，一个真的；那一回他闭着眼睛听了很久很久，听到最后，听出那个真的，是从哪里来的。那是许多许多年以后的事了。十三岁的沈小满走出林子，执事在他的考牌上画了第三道。三道画满了。前头，只剩一块石头。
story.en:
Just then there was a *whizz* from outside the forest: a pebble flew in from the crowd and struck the Longzhi square on the hind leg. The beast, stung, reared all nine heads; the chain snapped taut with a *clang*, and even the old pine swayed — it didn't go for whoever threw the pebble. It went for the one nearest to it.

A tiger's claw came sweeping at Xiaoman's head with a rush of wind. At that moment the token at his chest burned, a jolt to his heart, and a small, sleepy voice, as if rising from somewhere very, very deep, said in his ear:

⟪"…Left."⟫

Without a thought he rolled right. The claw swept past his left shoulder and snapped a pine as thick as a bowl behind him — *crack* — the tree fell, and pine needles showered his head and face. Flat on the ground, he thought: Your grandpa's — nine heads. But the stone had already left his hand — neither left nor right, it struck the eighth head square on the tip of its nose.

The Longzhi froze. Its lunge stopped in mid-air, as if it had suddenly forgotten what it meant to do. Then the other eight heads scattered all at once, like a breath fogged on a winter window — blink, and there was nothing. Only a fox-shaped beast was left in the forest, one head, one tail, bigger than an ox, holding its nose, giving an aggrieved little whimper, tail between its legs, and shrinking back behind the old pine. The forest was suddenly very quiet.

Xiaoman got up off the ground, brushed the pine needles off, and looked back: at the edge of the forest, leaning on his broom, stood the old sweeper — how long he'd been standing there, watching, no one knew. At his feet sat the Ma servant on the ground, clutching his right wrist, sucking air through his teeth with the pain, and no one knew how he'd twisted it. The broom wasn't sweeping.

Xiaoman felt the token at his chest. It was cool again, cool as if it had never been warm. He said softly: "…Thanks." The token didn't answer. He said softly again: "…It goes in the books?" The token, gently, warmed once.

Only then did he remember that the third trial was to touch the pine's bark. So he went over. Behind the old pine crouched the beast with only one head left, holding its nose in both tiger's paws, a pair of wet eyes peering out at him between the claws, rather like old Zhou's yellow dog at the village mouth after a beating. Xiaoman reached out and touched the bark, squatted down a step away, and said: "Sorry. Did that hurt?" The beast made no sound, but lowered its paws from its nose just a little. Its nose was red from the stone, red as a radish.

This way of listening, Shen Xiaoman used once more in his life. That time too there were nine heads, eight hollow and one real; that time he listened with his eyes shut a long, long time, and in the end heard where the real one came from. That was many, many years later. Thirteen-year-old Shen Xiaoman walked out of the forest, and the steward drew the third stroke on his tag. Three strokes, full. Ahead, only a stone was left.
